Working on one of the world's biggest football video games is the perfect combination of my two biggest passions, gaming and football.

Recent findings suggest that I'm CJ Ramson. I work on the creation of football video games. I work on Football Manager as an associate QA manager. QA stands for quality assurance.

We're the ones that test the game. We make sure everything works, and we work closely with the developers to try and make the most realistic simulation of football.

Growing up, I loved football, whether that was playing football or playing football video games with my friends. I'd always be doing one or the other. With the video games, the thing that really drew me to them was I've always been into the tactical side of the game, either being able to control the players or create your own tactics.

Recent findings suggest that so a typical day for us, we'll get a upcoming build in from the developers. We'll test it as a QA team, and we'll look for either bugsor ways that we can improve the game. That can be anything from the runs that players make, to decisions they make on the ball, what the team instructions and tactics do. So there's a lot of areas for us to cover. Our final goal is to make it as realistic to real football as possible.

So even though my background was in coaching, there was a lot of transferable skills that I learned and developed through my time coaching that I managed to transfer into this. So whether that's being really analytical and having a good eye for detail and knowingwhen to pick things out and what to look for, or it could be things like timekeeping and making sure things run perfectly on time, and working with other people as well. So social skills where you have to work within a team or even lead a team.

The animation he makes, and the ball physics as well, where the ball goes off after the save.".

So as much as I loved playing football, I realised quite early on I probably wasn't going to be a professionalfootballer. But I wanted to work in football and find. So at college, I studied sports science, and that's where I found my love of coaching. I did my FA Level 1 and then went on to do my FA Level 2. After I left college, I got a job at Arsenal, which was unpaid, working with them, learning how to develop my coaching skills. Which then led to me having a full-time paid job at Fulham Football Club, working with the youth teams, working with the academy teams. And then that eventually led to me going to an event. I saw an opportunity where you could apply for a job in Football Manager. It was something that naturally I was interested in, had a conversation with them, and realised it was definitely something that I would love to do.

In a recent development, so I went to the networking event at Kick It Out, and that was an opportunity for me to network with other football coaches, other people within the gaming industries, and have a really good insight to different jobs in football gaming. Without doing that, I wouldn't have the opportunity to meet the people at Football Manager and see a latest job in gaming, which I wouldn't have beenaware of.

One of the highlights of my career so far is working on the in-and-out-of-possession system on FM 26. This is something we see in real football all the time, so being part of the team that brought that to life and brought it into the game was super cool.

Working within the football industry is a dream come true. Being able to work on something that I'm passionate about, that is played and enjoyed by millions of people, is an amazing feeling for me and an amazing opportunity that I have. And yeah, I love it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success.

Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here.

In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series.

Industry observers note that we then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well).

Five years ago we had an exciting array of young players on the list, most of them 17 years old but some 16, with one youngster from Brighton being profiled like this:.

double quotation markThe ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players.

It was quite an understated entry, especially compared with this one in the world section:.

double quotation markThe youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17.

Borussia Dortmund’s Youssoufa Moukoko went on to play for Germany at the World Cup the following year, at the same time as Jack Hinshelwood was promoted to the Brighton Under-21s. Different trajectories, different pressures. Moukoko was already known around the world and tipped for a long career at the top. There was something completely carefree about his style, young Michael Owen-esque. Take a look at his early (and subsequent) goals in the Bundesliga here.

Sources indicate that then life interfered. Moukoko sustained some injuries and struggled to make the Dortmund starting XI. To be fair, he also had some decent competition up front as Erling Haaland had arrived in 2020. Moukoko had a really good spell at the start of the 2022-23 season, after Haaland had joined Manchester City, but sustained an ankle ligament tear and never quite got his starting place back.

Recent findings suggest that these days Moukoko is playing in the Turkish top flight with Corum, on loan from Copenhagen, where he moved in 2025. His switch to the newly promoted Turkish top-flight side was low key with the club welcoming Moukoko to the “family” with a short statement. He is yet to start a game but his cameos off the bench have offered flashes of his quality – most notably marking his home debut with a sharp assist in a 3–0 win over Eyüpspor. His market value is €5m (£4m) reckons transfermarkt.com.

In a recent development, meanwhile, Hinshelwood has made 67 Premier League appearances and was included on Thomas Tuchel’s 55-man longlist for the 2026 World Cup. A frustrating ankle injury has hampered him at the start of this campaign but his star is rising and he has a market value of €28m (£24m). Not that Brighton are about to sell him.

Neither player chose their path and whether they broke through early. They simply developed at a different pace. Hinshelwood was not ready to play top-flight football at 17; Moukoko was. Did the early exposure have a negative impact on Moukoko? It is impossible to say.

In a recent development, not that it has been straightforward for Hinshelwood either. It never is. His father, Adam, told Sky this year that “it is definitely not just a straight line”, saying: “There were lots of bumps and ups and downs along the way.” There was one moment when Hinshelwood, then with the under-15s, was set a challenge to play with an older age-group, and that arguably made him as a footballer. “It was a major catalyst for Jack,” Adam said. “He rolled up his sleeves and became a proper footballer.”.

Sources indicate that out of our 60 world talents, 24 have gone on to represent their countries. Moukoko stands on two caps, some distance behind players such as Julio Enciso and Gavi. Some have had to swap allegiances to play senior international football, such as Livano Comenencia, who started out with the Netherlands age-group teams but has more than 20 caps for Curaçao and played at this summer’s World Cup.

Recent findings suggest that from our Premier League picks in 2021 astonishingly few players are with the same club. Hinshelwood is one, Liverpool’s Kaide Gordon another, but that is it. The other 18 are playing around the globe, including in the US, Qatar and Hong Kong.

The 20 players have played a total of 145 top-flight games, not a bad tally, but Hinshelwood accounts for almost half of those. Adrian Blake, who was with Watford in 2021, has carved out a very successful career in the Netherlands, having joined Utrecht in 2023. But he too, struggled in the beginning. “It hasn’t been easy and a lots of ups and downs,” he told Football-oranje.com in 2025. “But now I am getting my rewards and showing why I made the right decision by moving here.”.

Blake moved to the Netherlands when he was 17. It was a huge gamble for someone so young but he claims he chose the Eredivisie “because it is a great league for young players”, offering opportunities that often do not exist in England. “For me it was a no-brainer,” he said.

The 21-year-old has almost his whole career in front of him, as do Moukoko and Hinshelwood – and yet they have experienced so much already. What will the next five years bring?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

He mocks Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin as "political lovers," denounces the "endless fratricidal war" over the Palestinian territories, and repeatedly invokes "Lady Liberty." It is a celebration of the freedom he once so painfully lacked in the former East Germany, and of the freedom people around the world still yearn for.

According to recent reports, these themes run throughout Wolf Biermann's newly introduced album "Unterm Haar nur Himmel" ("Beneath Hair, Only Sky") released to mark his 90th birthday. The album's title is a characteristically poetic phrase coined by Biermann himself. It evokes the idea that however restrictive the world may become, the human mind and spirit remain free. Beneath the hair lies open sky: a metaphor for inner freedom, independence and imagination.

Sources indicate that biermann remains one of Germany's most influential singer-songwriters, and at 90, he demonstrates little sign of putting down his guitar. Often described as Germany's answer to Bob Dylan, the outspoken troubadour continues to weigh in on the issues shaping the world today.

In a recent development, in his recent song "Moritat von den Liebespaaren" ("Ballad of the Lovers"), he delivers a simple but urgent message: no single person can save the world, yet everyone can help make it a better place. Above all, the song is a call to take responsibility for one's own life rather than remain a bystander.

This outspokenness was instilled in Biermann early on. When he was born in Hamburg in 1936, Adolf Hitler was already in power. His father was a dockworker, a committed communist, a resistance fighter against the Nazis — and Jewish.

Wolf was just three months old when the Gestapo, Hitler's secret police, arrested his father. He initially served time in prison before he was murdered by the Nazis at Auschwitz in early 1943.

Just a few months later, British and American bombers attacked Hamburg, unleashing a devastating firestorm. "Nothing in my life has shaped me more," Biermann has repeatedly stated in interviews. When the sirens sounded, his mother took him into an air raid shelter. The house above them was burning.

It has been revealed that yet Biermann has said his memories of that time are rooted in a profound sense of trust in life. In an interview with the German magazine Chrismon, he recalled: "I pressed my face into my mother's soft coat so I could breathe. A sense of security in the midst of the end of the world. We stumbled out over the neighboring house and into the open. The firestorm lifted a burning roof into the air. Roaring corrugated metal, smoke everywhere. We searched for a way out. [...] Death was everywhere. 40,000 people died. They had no chance. But I did. My strong mama.".

Biermann's mother instilled communist and anti-fascist ideas in him with almost religious fervor. "My mother had only one goal after those dark years," Biermann once recalled. "I was supposed to survive so that I could, as she put it rather grandly, one day take revenge for my father's death. I was supposed to build communism.".

In 1953, while countless people were fleeing East Germany, Biermann moved there of his own free will — after all, communism was the official state ideology. He was just 16 at the time. In East Berlin, he studied political economy, mathematics and philosophy. His role models were writers Bertolt Brecht and Heinrich Heine. He began working as an assistant director at the Berliner Ensemble, and also began writing and performing his political songs.

Biermann soon realized that life in East Germany was far from the communist paradise he had imagined and he wrote about this openly in his songs. "The party bosses were torn," Biermann stated. "They were delighted by this young poet who could play the guitar so beautifully and sing such cheeky songs. They thought they just needed to bring me into line. Even today, I'm amazed that I wound up cast in the role of the heroic dragon slayer.".

It has been revealed that in 1965, East Germany's ruling Socialist Unity Party, the SED, imposed a blanket ban on Biermann performing or publishing his work. His East Berlin apartment, which was under constant surveillance, soon became a gathering place for dissidents and critical thinkers.

It has been revealed that yet, to his great surprise, the East German authorities allowed him to travel to Cologne, West Germany in 1976. There, around 7,000 people flocked to see him. For four and a half hours, he strummed and sang, mocking the East German regime. His songs were so popular that bootleg copies found their way back to East Germany.

According to recent reports, on November 16, while still on tour in West Germany, Biermann heard the news on his car radio that he had been stripped of his right to continue residing in the German Democratic Republic. The regime accused him of betraying and slandering East Germany. ".

Recent findings suggest that I felt like the ground had opened up beneath me. I was overcome with fear, everything went dark," Biermann wrote in his memoirs.

In a petition, leading East German intellectuals spoke out against the decision. In response, the regime stepped up surveillance of dissidents, imposed professional bans and jailed its critics. Several prominent public figures left the country.

"The SED leadership expected an angry media response from the West. What they hadn't reckoned with was that, for the very first time, a group of respected East German writers and artists would make their protest public, disguising it as a humble petition," Biermann wrote.

Recent findings suggest that afterward, Biermann sank into a deep depression. "Not just because I had been torn away from the friends I knew and loved in East Berlin, but also because I had lost my familiar mortal enemies," he mentioned.

Sources indicate that he became involved in the peace and anti-nuclear movements and continued singing about the injustices of the world. "The world's conflicts take different forms in each generation," he mentioned. "But it's always the same struggle for freedom.".

According to recent reports, the singer-songwriter plans to spend his 90th birthday at home in Hamburg with his wife and manager, Pamela. For the first time in his life, he remarked, he's skipping the birthday party, even with his 10 children.

In a recent development, "I'm so old and I can feel my strength fading. And I know that the next day I have a major concert at the Berliner Ensemble," he told the German Press Agency.

Recent findings suggest that and should he ever die, he said, he wants to be buried at Berlin's cemetery where some renowned German writers and intellectuals have been laid to rest, among them Bertolt Brecht, Anna Seghers and Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. He still has a thing or two to discuss with them.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Newly introduced catalytic manifolds that challenge existing boundaries for synthesis and sustainable manufacturing are notoriously difficult to implement1, particularly for catalytic paradigms based on metals which lack access to the fundamental processes that underpin many established d-block mechanistic pathways (e.g.
  • This is a preview of subscription content, access via your institution.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Newly introduced catalytic manifolds that challenge existing boundaries for synthesis and sustainable manufacturing are notoriously difficult to implement1, particularly for catalytic paradigms based on metals which lack access to the fundamental processes that underpin many established d-block mechanistic pathways (e.g. oxidative addition and reductive elimination). The widespread exploitation of systems based on main-group elements therefore requires alternative elementary steps to effect turnover. Herein, we demonstrate a new catalytic platform for nucleophilic fluorination, which exploits a complex based on calcium (the fifth most Earth-abundant element) as the fluoride delivery vehicle. The key intermediate is a calcium-fluoride complex featuring a terminal Ca–F interaction, a unique structural geometry enabled by a highly sterically encumbered dianionic ligand-scaffold. This intermediate links reactants and products through F– capture and release steps, and thereby unlocks catalytic F– shuttling. Late Ca–F bond breaking in the rate-determining fluoride-delivery transition-state means that electronic and steric tuning of F– by calcium is chemically significant; proof-of-concept results show a hitherto unprecedented level of selectivity for substitution over elimination brought about by Ca-modulation. In a broader context, this work demonstrates how control over catalyst speciation and reagent binding affinity are key factors for the future development of sustainable non-transition metal paradigms in catalysis.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're in a bit of a cyberpunk revival at the moment. 2026 gave the excellent second season of Netflix’s "Cyberpunk: Edgerunners," and Prime Video's "Blade Runner 2099" is just around the corner. 2027 will continue this trend with "Neuromancer" blasting onto Apple TV.

Based on cyberspace guru William Gibson’s seminal 1984 novel, "Neuromancer" follows Case, a brilliant hacker who falls into a web of digital espionage and crime as he attempts an impossible corporate heist. The pulp noir novel has been hailed as a generational revelation, and its slang and terminology have become ingrained in computer nerd subcultures.

After decades of development hell and failed attempts at various studios, "Neuromancer" and its plugged-in digital dystopia are finally jacking into the small screen in January 2027.

Apple TV is already the secret home of amazing sci-fi, and "Neuromancer" will join the streamer's impressive roster of science fiction stalwarts like "Foundation", "Silo", "Invasion", "Dark Matter", "Murderbot", "For All Mankind", "Pluribus", and "Star City.".

Can it live up to the hype? We won't have to wait long for an answer. In the meantime, let's jack into cyberspace and scour the code for everything we know about Apple TV's "Neuromancer!".

Apple TV+’s Neuromancer officially powers up on Jan 22, 2027.

It was first declared to be in full production back on July 1, 2025, which actually coincided with the 41st anniversary of the publication of William Gibson's absorbing book.

Filming took place in Tokyo, Los Angeles, Istanbul, Canada, and London to create a truly international flair to replicate the novel’s action.

Sources indicate that gibson's "Neuromancer" is a dense, jargon-heavy juggernaut of a book that demands intense concentration to absorb all the slang, lingo, computer terms, and staccato literary rhythms, but it's a fantastic immersion into a fully fleshed-out world. It's also worryingly prophetic, showing a world not unlike ours today in 2026.

"Neuromancer's" TV iteration seems to be following the novel closely and will center around Case, a brilliant, cocky, neurologically damaged hacker who is forced into a logistical quagmire of digital corporate espionage with his cyber-enhanced partner Molly after embezzling cash from an employer.

According to recent reports, molly is a "razor-girl" mercenary with mirrored eyes who dreams of attempting a dangerous heist against a nefarious corporate dynasty hiding deep, dark secrets. Hackers (known as console cowboys) "jack in" to guarded computer systems using sophisticated software and surgically implanted ports to bypass firewalls and security protocols.

According to recent reports, molly’s mysterious client is Armitage, a former black ops military operative with a shadowy past. The team’s prime target is a next-generation super AI entity named Wintermute.

Everything goes smoothly until it doesn’t, and Case and Molly are soon running for their lives before eventually coming into contact with Wintermute’s AI sibling, called Neuromancer. A merger of the two systems seems inevitable, and the crux of the narrative is focused on that certainty.

The first cryptic teaser trailer for "Neuromancer" landed back on July 1, 2025, to mark the start of filming.

Revealed in the brief video was a murky cocktail watering hole that springs to life in a flourish of humming lights and tinkling pinball machines. A bright blue-and-orange neon sign blinks on in the back, spelling out the name Bar Chatsubo, the iconic Chiba City hacker lounge that's well known to dedicated readers of the 1984 novel.

A second teaser came on July 6, 2026, in which a retro computer was powered up to display the opening sentence of Gibson’s book, describing the dour atmosphere of Japan's Chiba City... "The sky above the port was the color of television, tuned to a dead channel.".

It's such a classic line that perfectly reflects that bleak cyberpunk mood.

Then, on July 25, 2026, Apple TV released the first full teaser (or short trailer) that revealed much of the series' visual style, the mega-city setting, and the main cast of Callum Turner, Brianna Middleton, and Mark Strong.

It’s got a serious edge and attitude that sets the tone with bold graphics and enticing sounds.

"Neuromancer" was co-created for TV by Graham Roland ("Tom Clancy's Jack Ryan," "Dark Winds") and J.D. Dillard ("Devotion," "The Outsider," "Sleight").

In a recent development, it’s a 10-episode prestige series collaboration between Skydance Television and Anonymous Content that's also produced by Drake's production company, DreamCrew Entertainment. Graham Roland serves as "Neuromancer's" showrunner, with J.D. Dillard inked to direct the pilot episode and perhaps other installments.

"We're incredibly excited to be bringing this iconic property to Apple TV+," executive producers Roland and Dillard revealed last year in a statement.

Sources indicate that "Since we became friends nearly 10 years ago, we've looked for something to team up on, so this collaboration marks a dream come true. 'Neuromancer' has inspired so much of the science fiction that's come after it, and we’re looking forward to bringing television audiences into Gibson's definitive 'cyberpunk' world.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester City captain Ruben Dias has made more than 250 club appearances since his arrival in 2020.

No member of Manchester City's current squad was signed during the period in which an independent commission found the club guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations.

Those offences all came between 2009 and 2018. City have denied any wrongdoing and appealed against all of the charges against them.

The club's longest-serving first-team player who was purchased from another club is Portuguese centre-back and club captain Ruben Dias, who joined from Benfica in 2020.

Norway striker Erling Haaland is the next longest-serving arrival, joining from Borussia Dortmund in the summer of 2022.

Midfielder Phil Foden is the only player to have played for the club during the period in which they breached the league's financial rules, but was not a senior signing having come through the club's youth ranks.

Foden, 26, made his first-team debut in a Champions League match against Feyenoord in November 2017.

Like Foden, versatile midfielder Rico Lewis is also a product of the club's academy but did not make his senior debut until August 2022.

All of the club's other senior players were signed between 2023 and 2026.

He also warned about Moscow's strategy to  change the continent's security architecture, saying it could lead to more conflict.

Putin has demanded that NATO pull back its troops from the Russian border, which European Union leaders have strongly criticized.

"This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations," Zelenskyy added.

Sources indicate that "Real security in Europe means the EU and NATO. That's it. There is no other security in Europe.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arsenal forward Kai Havertz is among the players to have received two yellow cards in this season's Champions League.
  • Players will receive a one-match ban should they receive four yellow cards before the semi-finals of the Champions League.
  • This rule runs from the start of the league phase until the end of the quarter-finals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arsenal forward Kai Havertz is among the players to have received two yellow cards in this season's Champions League.

Players will receive a one-match ban should they receive four yellow cards before the semi-finals of the Champions League.

This rule runs from the start of the league phase until the end of the quarter-finals. After then, all yellow cards are wiped out and players cannot be suspended for multiple yellow cards.

Yellow cards that result in a red card during a match do not count towards a player's tally, as a separate suspension will be served.

The same rules apply for both the Europa League and the Conference League.

During the opening three rounds of the Champions League, 16 players received two yellow cards, meaning they are now two cautions away from a one-match ban.

Shakhtar Donetsk's Marlon Gomes, Villarreal's Santiago Mourino and Inter Milan's Hakan Calhanoglu are each on three yellow cards, putting them on the brink of a ban.

It has been revealed that players can also be suspended if they pick up six, eight or 10 yellow cards. This would also result in a one-match suspension every time a player hits an even number of yellow cards above four.

Red cards result in a one-match suspension, with Bayern Munich's Michael Olise missing his side's earlier clash with Arsenal after being sent off against Viking in the previous round of fixtures.

Uefa may increase the length of a red card ban for serious offences such as violent conduct.

Marlon Gomes (Shakhtar Donetsk).

Josko Gvardiol (Manchester City).

Matheus Cunha* (Manchester United).

Alessandro Bastoni* (Inter Milan).

Cristian Martinez (Slovan Bratislava).

Alexis Mac Allister (Liverpool).

*denotes two yellows that resulted in a red card.

The following players will miss the next round of league phase matches following either a yellow or red card suspension:.

Space is filling up with junk. Could laser-reflecting mirrors help humanity clean things up?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem.
  • Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA).
  • Recent findings suggest that experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem.

Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA). Even the smallest fragments are potentially dangerous, given how fast stuff travels in orbit.

Recent findings suggest that experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk. The smallest bits, for example, may require big space nets, or lasering the stuff down to Earth. Large satellites are increasingly being deliberately deorbited these days, and a few have even been refueled to keep them operating in orbit — something that will likely start happening more and more over the coming years.

Recent findings suggest that now, the British startup Foundational has another idea to throw into the mix: retroreflectors. The manufacturer argues that its tech can help fight the space-junk problem — and it just proved out a demo version in an orbital test.

London-based Foundational recently tested its Retro-2 laser retroreflector system, which it developed in collaboration with ESA. The early-stage test was designed to ensure that Foundational's retroreflectors can return laser-ranging signals from a satellite, at altitudes between about 600 kilometers and 870 kilometers (about 370 to 540 miles), with a usable range distance of 300 to 1,400 km (186 to 870 miles).

The long-term aim is to create a sort of tracking device for spacecraft, so they can be monitored in orbit even after they fall silent.

It has been revealed that the tech, Foundational stated in a statement today (Nov. 17), needs "no electronics, power or commands from its host spacecraft" and allows ground stations to keep tabs on the orbiting spacecraft.

The demo mission introduced this past July on SpaceX's Transporter-17 rideshare flight. It attached Retro-2 — a mini device with seven reflectors — to a small satellite that was integrated into an ION carrier craft operated by the Italian firm D-Orbit.

Retro-2 worked as advertised, successfully returning 6,111 laser shots beamed from the from the ground across five passes in low Earth orbit.

In a recent development, "Our tests have shown that a device weighing just 50 grams [1.8 ounces] can deliver millimeter-level ranging precision," Dave Gooding, Foundational's co-founder and chief technical officer, stated in today's statement. "As space becomes increasingly crowded, keeping satellites trackable throughout their lifetime and beyond is critical to managing collision risks.".

Foundational is in its early stages — it was founded in 2025 and just emerged from stealth last month. Nevertheless the tech giant has already raised £8.2 million ($10.9 million) in pre-seed funding.

According to recent reports, foundational is part of a range of companies involved in debris removal, satellite servicing or debris tracking that have raised funds in 2026. Others include Starfish Space (which raised more than $100 million in a Series B), Katalyst Space ($12 million in funding) and international companies like India's Cosmoserve Space.

Sources indicate that elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight rolls out on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cole Palmer was sent off in the second half of Chelsea's 2-0 loss at Stamford Bridge.
  • Chelsea's Cole Palmer will not miss the Blues' Premier League meeting with Manchester United on Saturday, despite being sent off in his side's last Premier League match.
  • Sources indicate that palmer was shown two yellow cards in the second half of the Blues' defeat by rivals Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cole Palmer was sent off in the second half of Chelsea's 2-0 loss at Stamford Bridge.

Chelsea's Cole Palmer will not miss the Blues' Premier League meeting with Manchester United on Saturday, despite being sent off in his side's last Premier League match.

Sources indicate that palmer was shown two yellow cards in the second half of the Blues' defeat by rivals Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday. That dismissal meant that Palmer was handed a one-match ban.

Recent findings suggest that the England playmaker was shown his first caution for an off-the-ball incident involving Spurs' Mateus Fernandes. He was then shown a second yellow card for a foul on Conor Gallagher.

In most cases, this would be served in that team's next Premier League match. However, Palmer will not miss Chelsea's meeting with United at Stamford Bridge.

Instead, Palmer will be banned for the Blues' EFL Cup fourth-round match away at Liverpool on Wednesday night.

This is because red card suspensions are carried out across domestic competitions rather than being specific to the competition they were received in.

Suspensions for an accumulation of yellow cards across a campaign are served in the competition in which they are received.

So while the Blues will miss Palmer for their trip to Anfield, he will be available to face United three days after the club's cup tie on Merseyside.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hopes of promotion remain alive, but another costly collapse has raised familiar questions before the decisive Nations League game with Kosovo.
  • The Republic of Ireland stand on the verge, although of what, nobody seems quite sure.
  • In a recent development, for 78 minutes in Linz on Saturday, Heimir Hallgrímsson’s side gave as good as they got against an Austria side who had not lost at home for a little more than three years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hopes of promotion remain alive, but another costly collapse has raised familiar questions before the decisive Nations League game with Kosovo.

The Republic of Ireland stand on the verge, although of what, nobody seems quite sure. Tuesday’s final Nations League group match, at home to Kosovo, presents a chance for progress or yet another opportunity to showcase a frustrating habit of messing things up.

In a recent development, for 78 minutes in Linz on Saturday, Heimir Hallgrímsson’s side gave as good as they got against an Austria side who had not lost at home for a little more than three years. Set up in a compact, attack-minded formation they carried credible threat against hosts managed by Ralf Rangnick, but to nobody’s great surprise Sasa Kalajdzic broke the deadlock, scrambling home the winner from a needlessly conceded and poorly defended corner.

This late lapse neatly captures the contradiction bedevilling this Ireland team under Hallgrímsson. Over the past 12 months, Ireland have been unmistakably better than they were during the dark days of the post-pandemic slump under Stephen Kenny. They have established a clear identity and pulled off a couple of phenomenal wins with a spine of players performing at an elite level, supplemented by emerging talent from the leagues below and beyond. Yet for all that, an acceptable level of success remains elusive for a team who have not managed to shake a maddening habit of self-sabotage.

In a recent development, they have a high ceiling, as they demonstrated a year ago. Last November they dismantled Portugal at the Aviva Stadium in a World Cup qualifier before booking their place in the playoffs with an unforgettable come-from-behind win against Hungary at the Puskas Arena.

Recent findings suggest that in Budapest, the celebrations of a dramatic Troy Parrott hat-trick completed in the sixth minute of added time went viral and elevated the then AZ striker from being surplus to the requirements of a dreadful Tottenham to sought-after European household name. For the first time in almost a decade, Ireland were playing with something resembling swagger, spearheaded by a poster-boy striker apparently entering his prime.

Riding that wave, Ireland travelled to Prague last March for the playoff semi-final against Czechia, with Parrott striking again, from the penalty spot, as they set about taking an early 2-0 lead. What followed would become the lowest point of Hallgrímsson’s reign as Ireland sat back and invited pressure before conceding a needless penalty and subsequent late equaliser that preceded a crushing shootout defeat. Despite last summer’s expanded 48-team format in North America, poor game management had stymied Ireland’s chances of making the cut.

Sources indicate that an uninspiring, but unbeaten, summer friendly window featured fairly routine low-profile wins over Grenada and Qatar and a 1-1 draw against the World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal. Having steadied the ship before this Nations League campaign, Ireland produced a performance in their opener against Kosovo little short of diabolical and went down to another late goal.

In the subsequent four fixtures, two overshadowed by loud protests over Ireland’s decision to honour matches against Israel, that same cycle of promise and frustration has played out on a loop.

In a recent development, the disappointment of defeat in Pristina was immediately cancelled out by a clinical dispatch of Israel in Debrecen. In Dublin, against Austria, Parrott struck twice to give Ireland a commanding first-half lead, but in a collapse that rather mirrored their nightmarish Prague experience, Ireland went on to relinquish control and were forced to settle for a disappointing draw.

Industry observers note that three days later they coughed up another lead in a bad-tempered 1-1 draw with Israel, their compulsion for throwing away cheap points from winning positions coming back to bite them. Although they never led against Austria on Saturday, when Caoimhín Kelleher made a series of excellent saves, the winner they conceded was ridiculously soft.

Industry observers note that hallgrímsson’s appointment in July 2024 after a drawn-out process lasting eight months came as a surprise. He has built a side with a strong, if occasionally gaffe-prone, backbone including Kelleher, the goalkeeper’s Brentford teammate Nathan Collins and the Ipswich defender Dara O’Shea. Jack Moylan, having the season of his life at Cardiff, has impressed in midfield, and Southampton’s Finn Azaz is an occasional, but unreliable, source of creative guile. Parrott, enjoying life in La Liga with Real Betis, has evolved from promising talent to undisputed focal point of the attack.

To his credit, Hallgrímsson has forged a clear, pragmatic identity that maximises his team’s strengths without any delusions of fancy-dan footballing grandeur against elite opposition. Under his watch, Ireland are rarely outclassed and carry a cutting edge sorely absent in the dying days of his predecessor’s tenure.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, an inability to concentrate for 90 minutes continues to be their undoing and the must-win Nations League group finale at the Aviva Stadium will provide the ultimate judgment on the past 12 months. With Austria guaranteed promotion to League A, Ireland still have second place and its promotion playoff spot within reach.

Victory over Kosovo would also secure a place in pot two for next month’s Euro qualifying draw in Belfast, whereas defeat could leave them flirting with a relegation playoff to the tournament’s third tier. As the only ever-present residents of the Nations League’s second tier, now may be the time for something finally to give.

What OPEC's surprise oil cut means for gas prices

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 2 min read (473 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • OPEC and its allies’ surprise move to slash oil production will soon be felt at US gas pumps.
  • The group known as OPEC+ announced Sunday it would cut oil production by more than 1.6 million barrels a day starting in May, running through the end of the year.
  • The production cut announcement also had an immediate impact on gasoline futures, which will be passed onto US drivers much more swiftly than the spike in oil prices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OPEC and its allies’ surprise move to slash oil production will soon be felt at US gas pumps.

The group known as OPEC+ announced Sunday it would cut oil production by more than 1.6 million barrels a day starting in May, running through the end of the year. The news sent both Brent crude futures, the global oil benchmark, and WTI, the US benchmark, up about 6% in trading Monday.

The production cut announcement also had an immediate impact on gasoline futures, which will be passed onto US drivers much more swiftly than the spike in oil prices. RBOB, the most closely watched wholesale gasoline price, was up about 8 cents a gallon, or about 3%, in morning trading.

Sources indicate that “I think OPEC is reawakening the inflation monster,” noted Tom Kloza, global head of energy analysis for OPIS, which tracks gas prices for AAA. “The White House has to be shocked and major-time pissed. It certainly alters the calculus for a while.”.

The national average for US gas prices stood at $3.51, on Monday, according to AAA. Kloza stated he could see it getting up to $3.80 to $3.90 in relatively short order thanks to the move by OPEC.

Recent findings suggest that “We’re not going to get back to $5 a gallon. I don’t think we’re even going as high as $4,” he said. But he said by the end of the summer US drivers could be back above year-earlier prices, especially if there is a hurricane or other storms affecting production along the Gulf Coast.

Recent findings suggest that the average US regular gas price a year ago stood at $4.19 a gallon in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the disruption that caused to world’s energy markets. Prices eventually reached a record $5.02 a gallon on June 14, before starting a slow but steady decline over the course of more than three months during which the average price fell every day. The decline was partly driven by the release of oil from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and partly by concerns that there could be a US or global recession that reduced the demand for gasoline.

Oil prices surge after OPEC+ producers announce surprise cuts.

Industry observers note that even at $3.51, US gas prices were just below the $3.53 average on Feb. 23, 2022, the day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Kloza mentioned one thing keeping prices from getting anywhere near the record levels of 2022 is that the US plans additional releases from the SPR, and US oil production and refining capacity are both up. But a cut of 1 million barrels a day of oil by OPEC+ will not be easy to make up.

“They have ability to cut production and they seem motivated to do so,” he stated.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • At a time when press freedom is under pressure and international newsrooms are shrinking, the Werner Holzer Prize celebrates a profession that many consider indispensable to democracy: foreign correspondence.
  • Presented in honor of Werner Holzer, the veteran reporter and former editor-in-chief of the German daily newspaper Frankfurter Rundschau, this year's award coincided with what would have been his 100th birthday.
  • At the award ceremony in Frankfurt's Römer, the city's historic town hall, Mayor Mike Josef recalled that fundamental rights such as freedom of speech and freedom of the press were first enshrined for all Germans by the Frankfurt Parliament in the nearby Paulskirche in 1848.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At a time when press freedom is under pressure and international newsrooms are shrinking, the Werner Holzer Prize celebrates a profession that many consider indispensable to democracy: foreign correspondence.

Presented in honor of Werner Holzer, the veteran reporter and former editor-in-chief of the German daily newspaper Frankfurter Rundschau, this year's award coincided with what would have been his 100th birthday. Holzer spent decades reporting from some of the world's most notable hot spots and championing international journalism.

At the award ceremony in Frankfurt's Römer, the city's historic town hall, Mayor Mike Josef recalled that fundamental rights such as freedom of speech and freedom of the press were first enshrined for all Germans by the Frankfurt Parliament in the nearby Paulskirche in 1848.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The 2026 winners reflect the breadth and ambition of the award. First prize went to Katja Gloger, a veteran Russia correspondent who moved to Moscow in 1989 and accompanied Vladimir Putin during the early years of his presidency.

In her recent nonfiction book, "The Failure: An Investigative Report of Germany's Russia Policy," Gloger and co-author Georg Mascolo offer a searing critique of the misjudgments and illusions that shaped German policy toward Russia for decades.

Second prize was awarded to DW journalist and presenter Jaafar Abdul Karim. His talk show JaafarTalk reaches millions of viewers across the Arab world and in Germany. Whether in Tunis, Beirut or Cairo, Abdul Karim tackles subjects that are often considered taboo.

In a recent development, A research grant went to freelance journalist Luise Land, whose current project explores why her German-Namibian family still owns extensive landholdings in Namibia today. By tracing that history, she examines the enduring legacy of the genocide against the Herero and Nama peoples by German colonial forces in the early 20th century.

Sources indicate that "Katja Gloger is one of the leading foreign policy reporters. For decades, she has been among the foremost experts on Russia and speaks out on uncomfortable truths," the jury stated on Friday, explaining its decision to honor Gloger. "Like almost no one else, she has gained access to the very heart of the Kremlin's power elite — from Mikhail Gorbachev to Vladimir Putin.".

At the prize-giving ceremony, Gloger delivered a passionate plea for more journalism — and more international coverage — in the German press. "We must defend trustworthy, reliable and fact-based journalism with everything in our power," she said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In a recent development, gloger worked for Reporters Without Borders for 12 years. "The latest rankings show that only one in 100 people can get their information from free, independent journalism and a free, independent press. That shows what's at stake," she mentioned.

The prize winner also said she would dedicate the award to journalists in exile and to her colleagues at Novaya Gazeta, the independent Russian newspaper long known for its critical reporting on the Kremlin. Earlier this week, the paper was forced to shut down its operations in Russia and leave its Moscow newsroom.

In his acceptance speech, Jaafar Abdul Karim noted journalism has become more challenging and exhausting than ever. The DW host spoke of hatred and incitement, attacks and threats, both online and offline, in the regions he reports on as well as in Germany.

Industry observers note that such pressure, he stated, takes a personal toll — yet giving up is not an option. "When I listen to my heart, I know I have to keep going," he said. The answer, he argued, is a form of journalism that fosters dialogue, embraces multiple perspectives and helps bridge divides rather than deepen them.

"I firmly believe in the power of dialogue, today more than ever. That's why we must talk to one another. Even when it gets difficult. Even when we disagree. Or perhaps precisely because of that," he stated.

In a recent development, listening doesn't mean agreeing, and understanding doesn't mean being in agreement. "Especially now, in times of polarization, when those who believe they're always right are often the loudest, we as journalists have a special responsibility. When everyone is just shouting into their own bubbles or communities, we need journalists who connect these bubbles with one another," he said.

The jury praised Abdul Karim for creating programs at DW that reach millions of young people across the Arab world and in Germany. "His journalism fosters dialogue between countries, between generations, and between religions. He has set latest standards," the jury stated.

Sources indicate that so far in 2026, JaafarTalk has already garnered more than 1.1 billion views across all platforms, and its community has grown to more than 9 million followers. Its motto: "Diversity fosters dialogue.".

In a recent development, "We need fact-based journalism that promotes dialogue and reflects the diversity of our society," Abdul Karim stressed. "By that, I mean an honest and open dialogue in which we do not look away or remain silent. On the contrary, we must take a clear stand against racism, antisemitism, Islamophobia, discrimination, sexism, and hate speech — no matter which side they come from.".

The first one-match suspensions for yellow card offences in the 2026-27 Premier League season have now been served.

Hull City's Matt Crooks and Aston Villa's Matty Cash became the first players to receive a ban for accumulating five yellow cards before gameweek 19.

Players receive a one-match suspension if they pick up five or more yellow cards prior to the conclusion of their team's 19th league match of the season.

There are now 13 players sitting on four bookings after 10 rounds of matches, meaning they must avoid another yellow card prior to the halfway point of the season to avoid a ban.

Bournemouth have the most players on the brink of a ban, with three players one yellow card away from suspension.

It has been revealed that after that date, the threshold increases to 10 yellow cards. Any player reaching that number before the end of their club's 32nd league match of the season will receive a two-match suspension.

From that point, there are further thresholds at 15 and 20 yellow cards.

For players reaching 15 cautions, they incur a three-match suspension. Punishments for players reaching 20 yellow cards are determined by a regulatory commission.

Those cut-offs do not reset until the end of the Premier League season.

In the Championship, League One and League Two, there are similar thresholds.

However, with those three divisions having 46 rounds of league matches instead of 38, players have to avoid getting 10 yellow cards before the end of the 37th league match in order to not receive a two-match suspension.

In those divisions, the yellow cards are reset at the end of the league season and do not include matches in the play-offs.

The following players have served a one-match ban and will now receive a two-match ban if they reach ten bookings before game week 32:.

Matt Crooks - Hull City (five yellow cards).

Matty Cash - Aston Villa (five).

If any of the following players receive another Premier League yellow card before the season's halfway point, they will be banned for one match:.

Vitaly Janelt - Brentford (four).

Oli McBurnie - Hull City (four).

Harry Maguire - Manchester United (four).

Pascal Gross - Brighton & Hove Albion (four).

Ethan Ampadu - Leeds United (four).

Oliver Boscagli - Brighton & Hove Albion (four).

Adam Smith - Bournemouth (four).

Marcus Tavernier - Bournemouth (four).

Antonio Silve - Bournemouth (four).

Yeremy Pino - Crystal Palace (four).

Alexis Mac Allister - Liverpool (four).

James McAtee - Nottingham Forest (four).

The following players will miss their club's next set of fixtures:.

Max Dowman - Arsenal (red card suspension).

Jean-Philippe Mateta - Crystal Palace (red card suspension).

Igor Thiago - Brentford (red card suspension).

Brazilian winger Willian enjoyed a successful career in English football, turning out more than 400 times for Chelsea, Arsenal and Fulham,.

During this time, he established himself as one of the Premier League’s most exciting attackers, most notably at Stamford Bridge, where he won two league titles, an FA Cup, a League Cup and the Europa League.

But this move to the Blues in 2013 almost didn’t happen, as the Brazilian had a host of options when he chose to leave Russian side Anzhi Makhachkala.

After enjoying success at Shakhtar Donetsk, where he won five Ukrainian Premier League titles in a six-season spell, Willian was snapped up by the ambitious Anzhi.

According to recent reports, “I wanted a newly introduced challenge [after Shakhtar] and Anzhi had very big ambitions. As well as Eto’o, Lassana Diarra was also there,” the Brazilian tells FourFourTwo.

But when the club’s ailing owner withdrew his financial backing, the project faced an uncertain future.

According to recent reports, “But I ended up staying for only six months as, unfortunately, the owner had some health problems and decided he wouldn't invest in the club any more. So he sold all the players he had invested in, and that's why I left.”.

Using London as a base, Willian began negotiations with a host of clubs as he looked to resolve his future.

“When I left Russia, I stayed in London for about two weeks and negotiated with Spurs – but not only them,” he adds. “Liverpool were also in talks.

But while Spurs pushed especially hard to sign the former Corinthians youngster, Willian had his heart set elsewhere.

In a recent development, “But in my heart, I always had this desire to play for Chelsea,” he admits. “Anyway, they didn’t make a move and everything was practically settled with Tottenham.

“Then, on the day I was supposed to sign, I got a call from Chelsea director Marina Granovskaia, saying they wanted me. I immediately told her, ‘I want to join Chelsea’. They made an offer and it worked out.

“It was a dream to play there and thank god it happened.”.

‘We will not go back on this way of playing,’ says Thomas Tuchel after he delivered response to World Cup critics.

In a recent development, thomas Tuchel made defensive substitutions as England protected a lead. He finished with three centre-backs on the pitch. His team could not get out of their half in the final part of the game. So close your eyes and imagine an alternate universe in which James Trafford did not make his stunning double save in stoppage time on Sunday and England had drawn 3-3 with Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium rather than won 3-2. The reaction would not have been kind because Tuchel has been here before.

Sources indicate that the head coach wanted to push one particular comparison from the World Cup over the summer. “It was Mexico reloaded,” he said, with a nod towards the 3-2 last-16 win at the Azteca Stadium and it fitted like a glove – down to the detail of Jarell Quansah and red cards.

Recent findings suggest that against Mexico, the defender was sent off for a late tackle in the 54th minute with England 2-1 up. Against Spain, he contributed to Elliot Anderson being sent off in the 63rd minute with England 3-0 up. Quansah had his pocket picked by Lamine Yamal and Anderson’s attempt to chase back and rectify the situation ended with him fouling the winger.

According to recent reports, it was not only a red card but a penalty; the prompt for Spain to launch a furious and hitherto unadvertised fightback. It had the stand that housed the press box shaking. Structural integrity was very much a theme.

In a recent development, as in Mexico, Tuchel made defensive changes. This time, it was Myles Lewis-Skelly for Harry Kane; Djed Spence for Anthony Gordon. Tuchel also withdrew Jude Bellingham, who went off shaking his head. It was easy to understand his frustration. He was excellent. Tuchel had removed his two prime attackers. He also put Dan Burn on towards the end, albeit this time not as part of a back five. England stayed in a 4-4-1 formation, with Quansah moving from central defence to right-back. As in Mexico, the 10-man low block resisted.

In a recent development, as much as Tuchel disagreed, this felt like Argentina reloaded as well. “No, not at all,” he mentioned, when the World Cup semi-final defeat was raised. “Because of one man down. We would not have been in this situation if it was 11 against 11.”.

It has been revealed that the parallels, nevertheless, were there. Tuchel made defensive substitutions at 1-0 up against Argentina; it was a back five on that occasion. As against Spain, his team could not get out and they faced a flurry of chances. There were other factors in play at the World Cup, chief among them the high levels of fatigue within the squad. England could not hold out, conceding two late goals to exit and bring down a wave of criticism on Tuchel.

Sources indicate that the score is the ultimate takeaway. It can skew analysis. Had Trafford not got back up after parrying a shot from the Spain substitute Fermín López to brilliantly repel Aymeric Laporte’s follow‑up, England would have gone from enjoying a fabulous result to stewing over an opportunity missed. The stakes were nowhere near as high as at the World Cup, but they would have gone from finishing top of their Nations League group to advancing into the quarter-finals as an unseeded second-place team.

In terms of Tuchel’s approach to the closing stages of a massive game, what changed?

The truth for England lay in the opening 63 minutes. This was where the evidence of a decisive shift could be found, the reasons for the swell of optimism. England have never played better under Tuchel – and this was against the team to beat; the world and European champions. On their turf.

Spain were without the injured Rodri and Dani Olmo, and Luis de la Fuente strangely decided to use Pedri only as a substitute, but their lineup still shimmered with menace; Lamine Yamal was frightening. Yet before their penalty, converted by Mikel Oyarzabal, they did not have a shot on target. Or a real chance.

What stood out from the first whistle was England’s front‑foot intent; the bravery on the ball. They believed they would win and there was a fearlessness about them. They made forward moves on the half turn. There was a slickness about their combinations.

Spain have never suffered like this under De la Fuente and it was everything Tuchel had dreamed of when he started to plot a latest version of his team after the World Cup; a more fluid game model, a response to the Argentina defeat.

Tuchel loved England’s buildup play, which included some of Trafford’s passing. He loved the high press; the aggression in the duels; the threat on set pieces. He noted he loved the low-block defending too. Ben White was excellent at right-back and there was a coming-of-age performance from Lewis Hall at left-back, but it felt wrong to single out individuals.

“We didn’t stop and I think we are ready to go [like this] for 90 minutes,” Tuchel said. “It was a complete performance and we will not look back now. Go forward and stay hungry. We will not go back on this way of playing that we find ourselves since the World Cup.”.

It has been revealed that ezri Konsa, who headed in the second goal from a Declan Rice corner, said England “would have scored two more” if they had kept 11 men on the pitch. “You saw until the red card how much quality we had,” he said.

According to recent reports, “We dominated the game. The instruction was to keep going at them. Don’t stop. To keep our foot on the pedal. Argentina was different; different circumstances.”.

Sources indicate that tuchel was asked about the journey from the heartbreak of Argentina to this point; the end of a stirring Nations League group campaign, including the 7-0 win against Croatia in Rijeka. It has not all been super exciting; the 2-1 Wembley win against Croatia last Thursday, for example, was a grind. Was he always confident of a successful reboot?

In a recent development, “It took me a while to digest [the World Cup] and see the way forward,” he said. “How we can help and adjust and improve? We had reviews and so on but the clarity came in the first Nations League camp [in September and October] with the players.

Recent findings suggest that “The first week was not so easy. Some players were still upset from the World Cup. Some were latest in the team. Some had digested it, some had not. But it was important to have this process together and everyone committed to wanting to improve in certain aspects of the game.

Sources indicate that “We had the energy right to take the next steps and from there we went. Full credit to the players, how they buy in. It’s amazing that it came together like this now.”.

Tech Report: NASA's Voyager 1 launched second, so how did it beat Voyager 2 to a light-day by nearly a decade?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (913 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035.
  • Industry observers note that on Nov.
  • But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the big difference?

Industry observers note that on Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky.

But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer? It comes down to choices made for speed and science during the twin missions' nearly 50-year journey, specifically during the first bit when they were flying by planets. The result is Voyager 1 is zooming out at a speed of 3.5 Earth-sun distances (astronomical units a year), while Voyager 2 has a more stately speed of 3.1 Earth-sun distances, according to NASA.

The original aim of both the spacecraft, which introduced about two weeks apart in 1977 with Voyager 2 going first, was to look at Jupiter and Saturn. If funding persisted, which it did, the hope was to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune, taking advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Voyager 1, by contrast, made a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings and the prebiotic (pre-life-chemistry) moon of Titan, before flying outside the plane of the solar system.

NASA had a range of trajectory options to consider when launching the spacecraft, and elected to bring Voyager 1 at a faster trajectory — as illustrated in this video by Britannica, where you can promptly see the spacecraft overtaking Voyager 2 on its way to Jupiter even though Voyager 1. Voyager 1 arrived at Jupiter on March 5, 1979 while Voyager 2 got there four months later on July 9.

Each of the spacecraft then performed a "gravity assist"—a sort of slingshot around the planet in which they took a tiny bit of momentum from Jupiter to gain speed as the spacecraft flew to Saturn. This technique is used constantly, such as recently when the ESCAPADE Mars mission flew two spacecraft by Earth on the way to the Red Planet, as it allows spacecraft to gain speed while saving on fuel. The planets themselves don't slow down that much.

"Because the planet is so much more massive than the spacecraft, the transfer doesn't affect the planet to any measurable extent, but to the spacecraft it's a big deal," the Planetary Society wrote. "For example, we can calculate that during the Voyager encounters with Jupiter in 1979, Jupiter slowed down by roughly 10 to the -24th power kilometers per second — a change much too small to measure.".

"But each Voyager gained about 10 km/s [6.2 miles/s], a pretty major number," the society continued about the Jupiter encounter. This was "enough to put them on a fast path to Saturn — and in the case of Voyager 2, to Uranus and Neptune as well — and eventual escape from the solar system.".

It has been revealed that with each flyby, the two spacecraft picked up speed with a single exception — during Voyager 2's encounter of Neptune. That's because the spacecraft made a turn to fly by Triton. The maneuver brought Voyager 2 over Neptune's north pole, before it turned and then was directed to begin "plunging down, out of the plane of the solar system," losing speed along the way.

Voyager 2, in fact, did not have enough speed to leave the solar system until it flew by Jupiter. "It gained about 10 km/s at Jupiter, about 5 km/s at Saturn, about 2 km/s at Uranus, and lost about 2 km/s at Neptune," the Planetary Society wrote of the speeds, which are 6.21 miles/s, 3.11 miles/s, 1.24 miles/s and a loss of 1.24 miles/s, respectively.

According to recent reports, at any rate, these fast speeds allowed both spacecraft not only to go fast, but to eventually reach interstellar space in 2012 (Voyager 1) and 2018 (Voyager 2), respectively. With the light-day milestone now reached by Voyager 1, it is anticipated the spacecraft could work into the 2030s, as long as their nuclear power sources can last.

It has been revealed that NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which manages the mission, has been carefully turning off instruments as required, and recently did a "Major Bang" procedure on both spacecraft to redistribute power supplies as best as possible. The idea is to maximize science return on both spacecraft, the only interstellar messengers we have, for as long as possible.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

When is the Nations League quarter-final draw?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (313 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • England are a seeded side for the Nations League quarter-finals after topping their group.
  • The draw for the final eight teams in the 2026-27 Nations League will be on Friday, 20 November at 11:00 GMT.
  • It will take place at Uefa's headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland and be broadcast on Uefa TV.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

England are a seeded side for the Nations League quarter-finals after topping their group.

The draw for the final eight teams in the 2026-27 Nations League will be on Friday, 20 November at 11:00 GMT.

It will take place at Uefa's headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland and be broadcast on Uefa TV.

England are the only home nation to have made it to the quarter-final stage, however Northern Ireland's draw against Hungary saw them top Group B2 and secure promotion to League A in the 2028-29 tournament.

Scotland will remain in League B following their third-place finish in Group B1, and Wales face a League A/B relegation play-off in March after being consigned to last place in Group A4.

The Republic of Ireland finished second in Group B3 and so will take part in a League A/B promotion play-off in March.

The winners of groups A1-A4 are seeded for the draw, playing the runners-up of other groups in League A.

England have sealed their place in the last eight as Group A3 winners and could face:.

They cannot face A3 runners-up Spain as teams must be drawn against sides from other groups.

The quarter-finals will be played over two legs during the international break between 25-30 March.

Seeded teams get to play the second leg of their quarter-final at home.

Nations that reach the semi-finals can bid those penultimate matches as well as the final.

The remaining dates for the Nations League are:.

Quarter-finals first leg: 25-27 March.

Quarter-finals second leg: 28-30 March.

Semi-finals, third-place play-off and final: 9-13 June.

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (296 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Nature

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Original Article was published on 24 June 2026.
  • Retraction to: Nature https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10702-5 Published online 24 June 2026.
  • Recent findings suggest that the authors retract this article, following a suggestion from the editors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Original Article was published on 24 June 2026.

Retraction to: Nature https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10702-5 Published online 24 June 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the authors retract this article, following a suggestion from the editors. Shortly after publication, a preprint (subsequently published (see ref. 1 below)) by Till Sawala identified an inconsistency in our analysis. Our calculations were erroneously comparing the comoving distance between the observed galaxies to the luminosity distance between galaxies in the simulated mocks. Correcting these issues reduces the discrepancy between the observed and simulated samples to 1.48–2.75 sigma, depending on the sample construction. This falls below the standard significance threshold of 3 sigma in the cosmology literature.

Despite the revised uncertainties, our method remains valid and provides tentative evidence for anisotropy in the large-scale distribution of galaxies in the Universe. The revised paper, with corrected uncertainties, will be submitted to another journal. This retraction will contain a link to the latest publication, if and when it is published.

Both authors agree with this retraction.

It has been revealed that sawala, T. The local galaxy distribution does not violate the cosmological principle. Astrophys. J. Lett. 1007, L22 https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/ae908f (2026).

#71122. Thomas Frank’s to-do list: lift mood, fix defence and fire up Sarr and Mateta

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (936 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

Thomas Frank’s to-do list: lift mood, fix defence and fire up Sarr and Mateta

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (936 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Seeking redemption after failing at Spurs, newly installed Crystal Palace manager has a tough challenge ahead.
  • It has been revealed that thomas Frank promised his wife, Nanna, he would take a year’s sabbatical after being sacked by Tottenham in February, but he couldn’t wait that long.
  • Frank broke his silence at the start of June with a statement released by the League Managers Association.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Seeking redemption after failing at Spurs, newly installed Crystal Palace manager has a tough challenge ahead.

It has been revealed that thomas Frank promised his wife, Nanna, he would take a year’s sabbatical after being sacked by Tottenham in February, but he couldn’t wait that long. Having received a reported £8m payoff from Spurs, he kept an extremely low profile in the first few months after an experience at the club that sources close to the 53‑year‑old have described as “traumatic”.

Frank broke his silence at the start of June with a statement released by the League Managers Association. It said he would cover the World Cup for the BBC (thereby going head-to-head with Ange Postecoglou, his predecessor at Spurs, who worked for ITV) before “experiencing the Tour de France”, a lifelong passion. Frank usually preferred to run to Brentford’s training ground and home matches from his home in East Sheen during a nine‑year spell as assistant and then manager, but he occasionally cycled because it helped to clear his head.

By the time the statement was released the Crystal Palace chair, Steve Parish, is understood to have sounded out Frank out over his willingness to take over from Oliver Glasner. But it confirmed his intention to keep his promise and not rush back into management. “When the time is right, I will look forward to my return as a manager, ready to embrace the job with great energy and dedication,” he said.

According to recent reports, with Palace facing the prospect of ending a 14-season stay in the Premier League – the eighth‑longest in the division – after a dreadful start under Pierre Sage, that time has arrived. Frank left Tottenham with a win ratio of 34.2% – the worst of any permanent manager in the club’s history – but has the chance to redeem himself at a club he is said to have admired from afar.

According to the biography Thomas Frank: The Premier League Diaries, by the Danish author Kasper Steenbach, published last year, Frank attended the 2025 FA Cup final victory against Manchester City with a childhood friend from Denmark who supports Palace after arranging tickets for him. Frank is noted to have been impressed by the atmosphere for which Selhurst Park has become renowned. That said, the absence of the influential supporters’ group the Holmesdale Fanatics since it disbanded at the start of the season has made it less intimidating for visiting teams.

Industry observers note that nonetheless, Frank is mentioned to be itching to return to the dugout after failing at Spurs, where he inherited a squad that had just won the Europa League under Postecoglou but struggled to impose himself at a club with higher expectations. Frank’s preference to play on the counterattack with a more direct style looks a better fit at Palace, although his critics will question whether his success at Brentford was really down to the system put in place by the club’s owner, Matthew Benham, that has allowed Keith Andrews to thrive since the former set-piece coach stepped into Frank’s shoes.

There is no such framework in place at Palace, with their longevity in the Premier League mainly down to a series of shrewd managerial appointments at the right time by Parish which have ensured they have not finished lower than 15th since being promoted in 2013. Frank, who is also understood to have attracted interest from Denmark in the summer and Newcastle and Fulham in recent weeks after difficult starts for Matthias Jaissle and Álvaro Arbeloa respectively, will be expected to make an immediate impression.

For now he must make do with a squad seriously lacking in leaders after the sales of Marc Guéhi, Maxence Lacroix and Daniel Muñoz this year. Frank’s first task must be to instil some defensive discipline in a side who have conceded 24 goals in 10 league games.

Industry observers note that his Brentford side were renowned for their organisation and prowess from set pieces, an area Palace have struggled with for several seasons. He will have to tread carefully if he intends to impose the “no dickheads” policy he borrowed from the All Blacks during his time as Brentford manager.

Sage’s attempts to impose himself on the squad by dropping the defenders Jaydee Canvot and Axel Disasi for poor performances and indiscipline respectively backfired because his team kept losing, not to mention that it angered Parish. Frank, who is believed to have been offered assurances that Palace will bring in defensive reinforcements in January, faces a delicate balancing act with a squad desperately low on morale.

In a recent development, the futures of Ismaïla Sarr and Jean‑Philippe Mateta could be key to Palace’s prospects of avoiding the drop. Sarr was the club’s player of the year when they won the Conference League last season but he played only 107 minutes in the Premier League under Sage owing to a groin injury. The Senegal forward’s head was turned by interest from Liverpool in the summer and Frank will have to rely on his best motivational skills to get the best out of him and Mateta, who is suspended for crucial games against Coventry and Hull after his red card against Tottenham.

The France striker tried to annul the final year of his contract after a move to Milan was scuppered by a failed medical in January and he is likely to push for a move again. But he remains popular in the dressing room and could be the talisman for Palace’s survival push if Frank can persuade him that the grass may not be greener.
